flashcards.q: What does the forgetting curve tell us?
flashcards.a: Without review, we forget most of what we learn within a day.
flashcards.more: The brain does not keep everything. Whatever it does not need again, it drops quickly, and the drop is steepest in the first day. That is why a short review the day after learning pays off the most.

flashcards.a: Trying to remember the answer yourself, before looking at it.
flashcards.more: Re-reading only makes things feel familiar; the brain does no real work. When you try to remember, the brain has to dig the information out, and that digging is what strengthens the path to it. Flashcards and the quiz make you do exactly this.

flashcards.a: Reviewing a little every few days, instead of ten times in one day.
flashcards.more: A memory gets strongest when you review it just as you are about to forget it. So review today, tomorrow, in three days and in a week, letting the gaps grow. The Flashcards room helps here: the cards you mark as forgotten come back first.

flashcards.q: What are the four steps of the learning loop?
flashcards.more: See it on a slide, recall it with flashcards, check yourself with the quiz, and come back a few days later to run the flashcards again. Most people stop after the first step, which is why they forget.

flashcards.a: Taking in the same idea in two forms: a picture and words.
flashcards.more: The brain stores pictures and words along separate paths. When an idea is stored both ways, you can pull it back through one even if the other has faded. That is why almost every slide here has a picture.

flashcards.q: What are the three rooms of the platform, and what is each one for?
flashcards.a: Lesson teaches with slides, Flashcards make you recall, and Quiz checks you with explained questions.
flashcards.more: All three follow the same list of topics, so whatever you learn in Lesson you can recall in Flashcards and check in Quiz. There is no account: your reading progress and flashcard marks are saved in this browser.

flashcards.q: What is the shortcut to open search?
flashcards.a: Ctrl + K (⌘ + K on a Mac), or just press /.
flashcards.more: Type any word into search, such as "cache" or "payment". Results are grouped by topic and each one shows a one-line summary underneath, so you can tell which one you need without opening it.

flashcards.q: What is architecture in one line?
flashcards.a: The decisions that are hardest and most expensive to change later.
flashcards.more: Repainting a house is easy; moving a pillar is almost impossible. In software, the data model, service boundaries and public API are the pillars. Deciding them carefully up front is the architect's job.

flashcards.q: What is the main reason small apps break as they grow?
flashcards.a: The code doesn't change; the pressure does: more users, more data, more simultaneous requests.
flashcards.more: With 10 users, two people never press the same button at the same moment, so problems stay hidden. With 10,000, it happens every second. The hidden weaknesses then all come out at once.

flashcards.a: Checking the state first and changing it in a separate step — another request can slip in between.
flashcards.more: For example: "Is the seat free? Then book it." Because checking and changing are two separate steps, two requests can both see "free". The fix is to turn the two steps into one indivisible step. More in [[concurrency/atomic-operations/oversold-stock|atomic operations]].

flashcards.q: How do you stop two requests booking the same seat?
flashcards.a: Put the check inside the write: UPDATE … WHERE the seat is still free, then look at how many rows changed.
flashcards.more: Reading first and writing second leaves a gap. A single conditional UPDATE has no gap: the database checks the condition and changes the row as one step. If 0 rows changed, someone else won, so answer 409 "Seat taken".

flashcards.q: When does a race condition happen?
flashcards.a: When several requests read and change the same data at once, and the result depends on who gets there first.
flashcards.more: You'll never catch it by testing alone, because requests then arrive one after another. It shows up in production once the load rises, and the result is double sales or a wrong balance.

flashcards.q: What are the limits of a conditional UPDATE as a fix?
flashcards.a: It guards one row only, and it tells you just "0 rows", not why.
flashcards.more: When a rule spans several rows or tables, such as moving money between two accounts, wrap the steps in a transaction with a lock. See [[concurrency/atomic-operations/oversold-stock|atomic operations]]. A bulk UPDATE also skips entity events and leaves already-loaded objects stale.

flashcards.q: Where do slow jobs (emails, reports) get moved to?
flashcards.a: Into a queue; a worker does them later in the background.
flashcards.more: There's no need to keep the user waiting 4 seconds while an email goes out. The API just writes "this job needs doing" into the queue and responds immediately. The worker picks the job up in its own time.

flashcards.q: Button color or data model: which deserves more thought?
flashcards.a: The data model. A color changes in an afternoon; a data model takes months.
flashcards.more: One question decides how much time a decision deserves: "What will it cost to change later?" Make cheap decisions fast and slow down for expensive ones. Giving every decision equal time is the biggest beginner mistake.

flashcards.a: It keeps an answer so it can be served quickly instead of being built again each time.
flashcards.more: Computing something from the database is slow; reading it from memory is far faster. So answers that are needed again and again get stored in a cache. The hard part is deciding when a stored answer has gone stale.
